videos.title: Template Tuesdays #18 - Toolbar Tricks You Didnt Know In Chief Architect X18
videos.description: Live Template Tuesday session covering Chief Architect X18 toolbar customization, custom toolbar icons, toolbar configuration transfer workflows, temp backup extraction, and Pro Plan template updates.
videos.summary:
# Summary

This Template Tuesday session demonstrates advanced Chief Architect X18 toolbar customization workflows, including how to create hidden/toggleable toolbars, add built-in tools and custom library-object tools, create custom toolbar icons, and transfer toolbar definitions between configurations by editing exported `.toolbar` configuration files.

The session begins with a strong warning that the workflow involves touching Chief Architect configuration files outside the application. The recommended safety practice is to make backups, avoid asking Chief Architect support to troubleshoot self-modified configuration files, and only edit the narrow toolbar code sections that are understood.

The main workflow uses two helper programs: Notepad++ for inspecting and editing toolbar configuration text files, and TreeSize Free for finding the temporary Chief Architect backup directory while managed resources are being backed up. The key trick is that managed Chief Architect resources are temporarily decrypted into a temp directory during backup creation, and toolbar files can be copied from that temp directory before the backup completes and the temp files are deleted.

Inside Chief Architect, the video shows how to create a new toolbar by dragging tools into an empty toolbar area, rename the toolbar, control which view types it appears in, turn it off by default, and make it available as a right-click toolbar toggle. It also shows why floating toolbars should be docked before sharing configurations with other users to avoid toolbars opening off-screen on different monitor setups.

The video then demonstrates adding a custom Place Library Object button, linking it to an extended style painter library object, and assigning it a custom PNG icon. The icon workflow uses existing Chief Architect button resources as visual references, Photoshop or Photopea for editing, 128 x 128 transparent PNG output, and Chief Architect's browse button to attach the custom icon to the toolbar button.

The most advanced section shows copying toolbar definitions from one configuration file to another. The safe edit is to copy the line containing the toolbar's tool codes from a source `.toolbar` file and paste it over the corresponding line in the destination `.toolbar` file. The video warns not to rename the toolbar or edit the view-state code while doing this, because invalid codes can break the toolbar configuration and require a reset.

The ending covers related tips: adding toolbar-configuration-switch buttons to an existing toolbar, choosing icons for those configuration buttons, adjusting Chief Architect color preferences for dark mode visibility issues, understanding the basic structure of toolbar config files, resetting toolbars if they break, using Stream Deck or 3D mouse radial menus for hotkey workflows, and current Pro Plan X18 beta/template updates.

template tuesdays #18 - toolbar tricks you didnt know in chief architect x18 live template tuesday session covering chief architect x18 toolbar customization, custom toolbar icons, toolbar configuration transfer workflows, temp backup extraction, and pro plan template updates. # summary

this template tuesday session demonstrates advanced chief architect x18 toolbar customization workflows, including how to create hidden/toggleable toolbars, add built-in tools and custom library-object tools, create custom toolbar icons, and transfer toolbar definitions between configurations by editing exported `.toolbar` configuration files.

the session begins with a strong warning that the workflow involves touching chief architect configuration files outside the application. the recommended safety practice is to make backups, avoid asking chief architect support to troubleshoot self-modified configuration files, and only edit the narrow toolbar code sections that are understood.

the main workflow uses two helper programs: notepad++ for inspecting and editing toolbar configuration text files, and treesize free for finding the temporary chief architect backup directory while managed resources are being backed up. the key trick is that managed chief architect resources are temporarily decrypted into a temp directory during backup creation, and toolbar files can be copied from that temp directory before the backup completes and the temp files are deleted.

inside chief architect, the video shows how to create a new toolbar by dragging tools into an empty toolbar area, rename the toolbar, control which view types it appears in, turn it off by default, and make it available as a right-click toolbar toggle. it also shows why floating toolbars should be docked before sharing configurations with other users to avoid toolbars opening off-screen on different monitor setups.

the video then demonstrates adding a custom place library object button, linking it to an extended style painter library object, and assigning it a custom png icon. the icon workflow uses existing chief architect button resources as visual references, photoshop or photopea for editing, 128 x 128 transparent png output, and chief architect's browse button to attach the custom icon to the toolbar button.

the most advanced section shows copying toolbar definitions from one configuration file to another. the safe edit is to copy the line containing the toolbar's tool codes from a source `.toolbar` file and paste it over the corresponding line in the destination `.toolbar` file. the video warns not to rename the toolbar or edit the view-state code while doing this, because invalid codes can break the toolbar configuration and require a reset.

videos.title: Template Tuesdays #16  Moving and Placing Quickly With Precision
videos.description: Template Tuesday session covering precise movement, resizing, snaps, offsets, walls, doors, windows, backsplashes, cabinets, island layout, and extended cabinet styles in Chief Architect.
videos.summary:
# Summary

This Template Tuesday session focuses on precise movement, resizing, snapping, and placement workflows in Chief Architect. The video moves through walls, doors, windows, backsplashes, cabinets, island layouts, snap indicators, rotation points, offsets, and extended cabinet styles, with several side lessons on project management and Pro Plan toolbars.

The session opens with a quick Windows PowerToys tip for screen docking and then answers live questions about importing Rabbitt Design toolbars into Chief Architect X18 and switching project layouts after starting a plan. The layout-switching workflow uses project management copies, document folders, and the Reference Plan Layout tool to reassociate a layout with the correct plan file.

The core precision section starts with walls. It explains why most wall precision should come from dimensions after drawing rooms, then shows how to use CAD lines, polar coordinates, and the Tab/Enter coordinate dialog to create exact reference geometry. It also covers wall edit handles, resizing walls about the inner surface versus main layer outside, reversing wall layers, understanding interior/exterior wall sides, and resizing multiple exterior walls while preserving measured interior dimensions.

The next section covers doors and windows. It demonstrates concentric resize, setting jump distances for 2-inch door increments, using the `C` or comma key for temporary concentric resizing, changing door heights in 3D, setting matching window head heights, and changing room/default plate heights from an exterior room selection.

The video then moves into 3D resize workflows for backsplashes and cabinets. It shows how to resize a backsplash to surrounding objects by typing `0`, why drawing one clean backsplash rectangle can be easier than fixing automatically created breaks, and how to use the cabinet dimension edit subtool to choose between moving an object and moving/resizing an edge.

The cabinet section is the largest part of the session. It covers precise cabinet placement in plan and 3D, copy/paste placement instead of repeated click placement, moving cabinets exact distances from surrounding objects, reflecting cabinets, using multiple copy for island layout, applying Rabbitt Design style-palette tools by marquee selection, suppressing automatic fillers, using modular 3-inch cabinet increments, and centering ranges or cabinet groups between two points.

The later section explains Chief Architect snap indicators and how midpoint, center, endpoint, primary, and secondary snap colors help verify precise placement. It also demonstrates placing points as rotate/resize centers, rotating objects around a placed point, using multiple copy with rotation to create array-like patterns, and using copy/paste resize handles to create precise offsets.

The session ends with a live question about extended cabinet styles. It builds an Extended Style Painter style palette for base, wall, and full-height cabinets, applies it to a cabinet near a wall, turns on bumping/pushing for precise movement, and shows how extended style fields can report in a cabinet schedule. The closing note discusses Pro Plan X18 beta status, missing pony wall library objects, layer-based fill style updates, and plans to continue the precision movement topic in a future Template Tuesday.

template tuesdays #16  moving and placing quickly with precision template tuesday session covering precise movement, resizing, snaps, offsets, walls, doors, windows, backsplashes, cabinets, island layout, and extended cabinet styles in chief architect. # summary

this template tuesday session focuses on precise movement, resizing, snapping, and placement workflows in chief architect. the video moves through walls, doors, windows, backsplashes, cabinets, island layouts, snap indicators, rotation points, offsets, and extended cabinet styles, with several side lessons on project management and pro plan toolbars.

the session opens with a quick windows powertoys tip for screen docking and then answers live questions about importing rabbitt design toolbars into chief architect x18 and switching project layouts after starting a plan. the layout-switching workflow uses project management copies, document folders, and the reference plan layout tool to reassociate a layout with the correct plan file.

the core precision section starts with walls. it explains why most wall precision should come from dimensions after drawing rooms, then shows how to use cad lines, polar coordinates, and the tab/enter coordinate dialog to create exact reference geometry. it also covers wall edit handles, resizing walls about the inner surface versus main layer outside, reversing wall layers, understanding interior/exterior wall sides, and resizing multiple exterior walls while preserving measured interior dimensions.

the next section covers doors and windows. it demonstrates concentric resize, setting jump distances for 2-inch door increments, using the `c` or comma key for temporary concentric resizing, changing door heights in 3d, setting matching window head heights, and changing room/default plate heights from an exterior room selection.

the video then moves into 3d resize workflows for backsplashes and cabinets. it shows how to resize a backsplash to surrounding objects by typing `0`, why drawing one clean backsplash rectangle can be easier than fixing automatically created breaks, and how to use the cabinet dimension edit subtool to choose between moving an object and moving/resizing an edge.

the cabinet section is the largest part of the session. it covers precise cabinet placement in plan and 3d, copy/paste placement instead of repeated click placement, moving cabinets exact distances from surrounding objects, reflecting cabinets, using multiple copy for island layout, applying rabbitt design style-palette tools by marquee selection, suppressing automatic fillers, using modular 3-inch cabinet increments, and centering ranges or cabinet groups between two points.

the later section explains chief architect snap indicators and how midpoint, center, endpoint, primary, and secondary snap colors help verify precise placement. it also demonstrates placing points as rotate/resize centers, rotating objects around a placed point, using multiple copy with rotation to create array-like patterns, and using copy/paste resize handles to create precise offsets.

the session ends with a live question about extended cabinet styles. it builds an extended style painter style palette for base, wall, and full-height cabinets, applies it to a cabinet near a wall, turns on bumping/pushing for precise movement, and shows how extended style fields can report in a cabinet schedule. the closing note discusses pro plan x18 beta status, missing pony wall library videos.title: Template Tuesdays #15 - X18's New Project Information
videos.description: Template Tuesday session covering Chief Architect X18's new Project Information system, macros, title block workflows, layer-based fill styles, cladding, and Pro Plan template systems.
videos.summary:
# Summary

This Template Tuesday session explores Chief Architect X18's new Project Information system and how it can become more than basic client/designer metadata. The video demonstrates adding custom project information fields, inserting those values into text and note macros, and using the system as a foundation for title blocks, project information sheets, automatic annotations, specification blocks, and future Pro Plan template systems.

The first half focuses on creating and using project information fields. A custom `Scope of Work` field is added under the Project heading, filled with a project-specific value, and inserted into text and note objects from Chief Architect's macro dropdown. The video explains the macro syntax, why exact names matter, and how these values can be reused anywhere text macros are supported.

The video then moves into a title block and project information workflow. It shows how Rabbitt Design's Pro Plan uses a separate plan file to drive title block data, logo, stamp, design load criteria, and spec writing across multiple layouts. The new Project Information system can replace older custom parsing systems that relied on colon-delimited values and custom fonts, although custom scripting still matters when blank fields need to disappear automatically or when bold headings and normal values must be mixed in a generated text block.

The session also demonstrates using AI to quickly generate macro text from screenshots, discusses the limits of Chief's Project Information dialog such as no word wrapping and no sort order, and explains how project information could support reusable design annotations such as tile pattern notes, starter tile notes, and library objects that pull in project-specific values.

The second half branches into Chief Architect X18 beta features. It gives a deep demonstration of layer-based fill styles, including wall layers, roof planes, framing members, foundation walls, poche fills, wall hatching, and active view display control. template tuesdays #15 - x18's new project information template tuesday session covering chief architect x18's new project information system, macros, title block workflows, layer-based fill styles, cladding, and pro plan template systems. # summary

this template tuesday session explores chief architect x18's new project information system and how it can become more than basic client/designer metadata. the video demonstrates adding custom project information fields, inserting those values into text and note macros, and using the system as a foundation for title blocks, project information sheets, automatic annotations, specification blocks, and future pro plan template systems.

the first half focuses on creating and using project information fields. a custom `scope of work` field is added under the project heading, filled with a project-specific value, and inserted into text and note objects from chief architect's macro dropdown. the video explains the macro syntax, why exact names matter, and how these values can be reused anywhere text macros are supported.

the video then moves into a title block and project information workflow. it shows how rabbitt design's pro plan uses a separate plan file to drive title block data, logo, stamp, design load criteria, and spec writing across multiple layouts. the new project information system can replace older custom parsing systems that relied on colon-delimited values and custom fonts, although custom scripting still matters when blank fields need to disappear automatically or when bold headings and normal values must be mixed in a generated text block.

the session also demonstrates using ai to quickly generate macro text from screenshots, discusses the limits of chief's project information dialog such as no word wrapping and no sort order, and explains how project information could support reusable design annotations such as tile pattern notes, starter tile notes, and library objects that pull in project-specific values.

the second half branches into chief architect x18 beta features. it gives a deep demonstration of layer-based fill styles, including wall layers, roof planes, framing members, foundation walls, poche fills, wall hatching, and active view display control. it also shows x18 cladding and roof material improvements, custom low-poly cladding materials, brick depth variation, grass regions, window videos.title: Template Tuesdays #14 - Managed Mode Tricks and Tips
videos.description: Template Tuesday session covering Chief Architect Managed Mode, project export/import, team workflows, project browser tags, assets, archives, backups, plan references, and project recovery.
videos.summary:
# Summary

This Template Tuesday session explains Chief Architect Managed Mode, why it is valuable for teams and cloud workflows, and how to use it safely and efficiently. The video argues that Managed Mode is the best way to work with a team because it bundles project files, layouts, linked files, materials, assets, and support documents into portable project files while reducing the old plan/layout/backup juggling workflow.

The first section explains how Managed Mode stores and migrates settings, toolbars, libraries, and project data into encrypted files under Windows program/app data locations. It warns that manually copying those encrypted files can duplicate a machine but may also cause cache or write issues, so the safer path is to use Chief's Managed Mode export/import tools.

The video then demonstrates exporting a `.caproj` file, choosing which linked resources to include, deleting and reimporting the project, opening `.caproj` contents with 7-Zip, and understanding why files can become large. The main file-size culprit is usually image assets and material texture maps, including large PNGs and HDRI backdrops. The video explains ways to reduce file size by lowering texture resolution or managing secondary maps, while preserving rendering quality where needed.

The middle section focuses on Pro Plan and project-template workflows. It explains copying layouts with linked plan files into new projects, using a separate logo/design criteria/spec plan to drive title block and layout content, replacing reference plan layouts for different builders or jurisdictions, merging unused plan materials to reduce file bloat, and avoiding broken references by using `Make a Copy With Links` instead of ordinary copy.

The session also covers design iteration management in Managed Mode. It shows using new folders, separate projects, project tags/filters, active/hold/inactive/archive categories, open-project filtering, and thumbnail images to help a team understand and share different versions or options. It also gives a detailed architectural file naming convention based on date, version, project name, and initials.

The later section explains archive recovery, backup management, asset management, project references, and cleanup. It shows how to rebuild a project from archived plan/layout files, why renaming layout files matters, how Managed Mode backups grow when projects and assets accumulate, where cached files live, why downloaded manufacturer catalogs and imported project assets slow backups, and why a periodic library/project export plus asset purge can be worth doing.

The session ends by showing plan references for as-built/proposed workflows, replacing linked reference plans, repairing broken project references, saving thumbnail images for design options, and reminding users that Managed Mode has a learning curve but gives a cleaner workflow once a system is established.

template tuesdays #14 - managed mode tricks and tips template tuesday session covering chief architect managed mode, project export/import, team workflows, project browser tags, assets, archives, backups, plan references, and project recovery. # summary

this template tuesday session explains chief architect managed mode, why it is valuable for teams and cloud workflows, and how to use it safely and efficiently. the video argues that managed mode is the best way to work with a team because it bundles project files, layouts, linked files, materials, assets, and support documents into portable project files while reducing the old plan/layout/backup juggling workflow.

the first section explains how managed mode stores and migrates settings, toolbars, libraries, and project data into encrypted files under windows program/app data locations. it warns that manually copying those encrypted files can duplicate a machine but may also cause cache or write issues, so the safer path is to use chief's managed mode export/import tools.

the video then demonstrates exporting a `.caproj` file, choosing which linked resources to include, deleting and reimporting the project, opening `.caproj` contents with 7-zip, and understanding why files can become large. the main file-size culprit is usually image assets and material texture maps, including large pngs and hdri backdrops. the video explains ways to reduce file size by lowering texture resolution or managing secondary maps, while preserving rendering quality where needed.

the middle section focuses on pro plan and project-template workflows. it explains copying layouts with linked plan files into new projects, using a separate logo/design criteria/spec plan to drive title block and layout content, replacing reference plan layouts for different builders or jurisdictions, merging unused plan materials to reduce file bloat, and avoiding broken references by using `make a copy with links` instead of ordinary copy.

the session also covers design iteration management in managed mode. it shows using new folders, separate projects, project tags/filters, active/hold/inactive/archive categories, open-project filtering, and thumbnail images to help a team understand and share different versions or options. it also gives a detailed architectural file naming convention based on date, version, project name, and initials.

the later section explains archive recovery, backup management, asset management, project references, and cleanup. it shows how to rebuild a project from archived plan/layout files, why renaming layout files matters, how managed mode backups grow when projects and assets accumulate, where cached files live, why downloaded manufacturer catalogs and imported project assets slow backups, and why a periodic library/project export plus asset purge can be worth doing.

the session ends by showing plan references for as-built/proposed workflows, replacing linked reference plans, repairing broken project references, saving thumbnail images for design options, and
